_meta.note: Component efficiencies and masses used by the model. Every entry carries a `kind` field: 'literature' or 'datasheet' means the figure is quoted from the named source; 'estimate' means it is an engineering judgement and should be treated as uncertain. Prices are street prices observed in November 2026 and will drift.

generators.label: Schaeffler/Heinzmann Free Drive pedal alternator (1:29 cyclone gearbox)
generators.source: Schaeffler states Free Drive is 'approximately 5% less efficient than chain drives' (to Electrek, 2021-08-31). Back-solving that at typical assist levels gives 81-89% system efficiency; the component-level figure is not published. Heinzmann brochure ED_FDS_001_21_08_e confirms a 1:29 cyclone gearbox, 250 W continuous, 1200 W peak.
generators.note: The 5% figure is a system claim about battery range, not a drivetrain efficiency measurement -- see docs/crank-alternator-efficiency.md for why the two differ. No manufacturer publishes a generator efficiency curve.

generators.label: CIXI PERS Standalone pedal generator (cargo/urban)
generators.source: CIXI PERS KIT Catalog 2026, PERS Standalone spec table: 'Efficiency higher than 80%', 360 W continuous, 2000 W peak, 185 Nm, 100 rpm, 48 V.
generators.note: The only manufacturer in this survey publishing a generator efficiency number at all. Note it is a '>' bound, not a curve.

generators.label: Tournon series-hybrid bicycle prototype, simulated efficiency
generators.source: Tournon (2020), doctoral thesis, Universite de Lyon / ESTACA, 'Conception optimale d'un velo a architecture hybride serie et a base de supercondensateurs'. A prototype built mostly from off-the-shelf parts simulated at 36% on a hilly route; the best optimised design reached 73% on the flat without stops, and 62% with a 50 m climb.
generators.kind_extra: measured on a real build, but the figure is a simulation of that build
generators.note: The most directly relevant data point in existence: a real series-hybrid bike, built and simulated by the person who did the sizing theory.

generators.label: Car alternator, peak (near 2/3 of rated load, 2000-6000 rpm)
generators.source: SAE 2012-01-1058 puts automotive alternator peak conversion at ~47%; trade sources quote 55-60% typical, 68-75% for high-efficiency units.
generators.note: Requires roughly 30:1 step-up from an 80 rpm cadence to reach its efficient shaft-speed band.

generators.label: Car alternator at ~15% of rated load (150-250 W from a 1.4 kW machine)
generators.source: Derived: fixed iron, windage and field-excitation losses dominate at low load. Alternators are optimised for high load; part-load efficiency falls steeply.
generators.note: Also wound-field, so it needs field current and a voltage reference to produce output at all.

generators.label: Bicycle hub dynamo (Schmidt SON 28 class)
generators.source: Cyclingabout dynamo drag testing: SON 28 ~0.25-1.25 W drag for ~3 W electrical output in the 10-30 km/h band.
generators.note: Efficiency falls further below ~15 km/h. Best-in-class, and nowhere near 90%.

generators.label: Direct-drive hub motor used as a PMG (belt-driven from cranks)
generators.source: DD hub motors peak around 85-90% in their designed speed/torque region; a 3:1 belt step-up lets it sit there.
generators.note: Attractive because the controller already knows how to run it in regen mode.

generators.label: Purpose-built axial-flux PMG at design point
generators.source: Typical small axial-flux PM machine efficiency at rated load; falls off outside the design speed.
generators.note: No field winding, so it self-excites: no bootstrap problem.

electronics.label: 3-phase rectifier (synchronous or schottky)
electronics.source: Diode bridge at these currents; synchronous rectification does better.

electronics.label: DC bus / DC-DC conversion stage
electronics.source: A cap bank's 2:1 voltage swing forces either a wide-input controller or this stage.

electronics.label: Motor controller (FOC, part load)
electronics.source: Typical FOC controller; part-load and low-speed operation is worse than the headline figure.

electronics.label: LiFePO4 charge/discharge round trip
electronics.source: Cell plus BMS round-trip at modest C-rate. Only applies to builds that route pedal power through the pack; a direct-bus build bypasses it.

motors.label: Hub motor driving the wheel at ~200 W
motors.source: DD hub motors are quoted 85-90% peak; at 200 W in a 250-500 W motor you are at part load.
motors.note: This 90% figure in the original premise is the one part of it that holds up.

mechanical.label: Chain/belt stage (derailleur or IGH drivetrain)
mechanical.source: Well-established: chain drives run 95-99% per stage; a clean derailleur drivetrain is at the top of that band.
mechanical.note: This is the thing being replaced.

storage.label: Maxwell BMOD0165 P048 supercapacitor module
storage.source: EVEA (FR) listing: MAXWELL 48V 165F module, 14.2 kg, 1785.37 EUR ex-VAT. Datasheet energy 53 Wh.
storage.note: Retail modules carry a large markup over bare cells.

storage.label: 16 V 500 F ultracapacitor module (6 x 3000 F cells)
storage.source: DigiKey SM0500-016-PT-1 datasheet: 17.8 Wh, 3.1 Wh/kg cell-level, 2.1 mOhm ESR. Price from LiFoo listing.
storage.note: Mass estimated from the 3.1 Wh/kg cell-level figure.

storage.label: Maxwell BCAP3000 3000 F 2.7 V cell
storage.source: 0.5*C*V^2 = 10,935 J = 3.04 Wh. Street price observed 40-106 USD/cell depending on source.
storage.note: 18 in series gives 48.6 V / 166.7 F / 53 Wh. Needs balancing.

storage.label: 48 V 20 Ah LiFePO4 ebike pack
storage.source: BtrPower 48V 20Ah LiFePO4: 5.4 kg, 189.99 USD. Cycle life 3000-5000 cycles to 80%.
storage.note: The comparison point for cost and mass.

vehicle.mass_note: Rider (~78 kg) + bike + kit. Change it in the model; it scales linearly.
vehicle.crr_note: Typical for good tyres on asphalt.
